lessons.title: What a script is, and running one
lessons.summary: A script is a file of commands. Here's how to run it and why it sometimes refuses.

blocks.text: Everything you've typed so far went to bash, the shell: the program that reads your commands and runs them. A bash script is just those same commands saved in a text file, so you can run them all again with one command. Every Slurm job you submit is a script.

example.note: Line 1, the shebang (`#!`), says which program runs the file. Lines starting with `#` are comments for people. The rest are ordinary commands.

flags: Needs execute permission (x). The ./ means 'the file in this folder'

blocks.text: `./count_designs.sh` gives `Permission denied` until the file is executable. Give it x with `chmod +x`, then it runs.

try.text: Make the script executable, then run it with `./`.

quiz.q: Why does typing just `count_designs.sh` (without ./) say `command not found`?
options: The shell only looks for commands in PATH folders, not the current folder
quiz.why: The shell searches the folders in PATH. ./ tells it the program is right here.

lessons.title: Giving a script arguments
lessons.summary: Make one script work on any folder or file.

blocks.text: Arguments are the words after a command: in `ls runs`, `runs` is an argument. Scripts take arguments too. Inside the script, `$1` is the first argument, `$2` the second, and `$#` how many there are.

try.text: Write `count.sh` that counts the PDBs in the folder given as `$1`, then run it on `runs/run2`.
try.hint: nano count.sh, write: ls $1/*.pdb | wc -l, save with Ctrl+O, exit with Ctrl+X, then bash count.sh runs/run2

quiz.q: You run `./prep.sh il7r 8`. Inside prep.sh, what is `$2`?
quiz.why: $1 is the first word after the script name (il7r), $2 the second (8).

lessons.title: Saving output: >, >> and 2>
lessons.summary: Send output to a file instead of the screen.

blocks.text: Programs print two streams: normal output (stdout) and error messages (stderr). Both go to your screen unless you redirect them.

flags: Write normal output to file, replacing what was there
Add normal output to the end of file
Send output into another command instead of a file

try.text: Save the list of designs to `list.txt` instead of printing it.
Add the contents of `runs/run1` to the end of `list.txt`.
try.hint: ls runs/run1 >> list.txt  (two >, so it adds instead of replacing)

blocks.warn: A single `>` empties the file before writing. `ls runs/run1 > list.txt` would wipe the list you built. Use `>>` to add.

quiz.q: A script prints results and some error messages. How do you keep the errors in `errors.log` and still see the results?
quiz.why: 2> redirects only stream 2, the errors. Normal output still goes to the screen.

lessons.title: Writing scripts in nano, with variables
lessons.summary: Edit text right in the terminal, and keep settings in one place.

command.name: nano
command.what: Opens FILE for editing in the terminal (or a new empty file). Type normally. The bottom lines list the shortcuts; ^ means the Ctrl key.

flags: Save; press Enter to keep the name
Leave nano; it asks to save if you changed something

blocks.text: A variable holds a value you can reuse. Set it with `NAME=value` (no spaces around =) and use it with `$NAME`. Put settings at the top of a script as variables, so changing a target means changing one line.

example.note: Change TARGET=il7r to TARGET=pdl1 and the whole script follows.

try.text: Create `hello.sh` in nano with two lines, `#!/bin/bash` and `echo hello`, save it, and run it with bash.

tasks.text: Save hello.sh with an echo line

try.hint: nano hello.sh, type the two lines, Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X, then bash hello.sh

quiz.q: Which line sets a variable correctly in bash?
quiz.why: No spaces around =, and no $ when setting. The $ is only for reading the value.

lessons.title: Doing it to every file: for loops
lessons.summary: Repeat a command for each file or folder.

blocks.text: A for loop runs the same commands once for each item in a list, with a variable holding the current item. With a wildcard, the list is every matching file.

example.cmd: for f in designs/*.pdb; do echo $f; done
example.note: Read it as: for each file f matching designs/*.pdb, do echo $f. `done` ends the loop. The `;` separates the parts on one line.

try.text: Count the PDBs in each run folder with a loop.
try.hint: for r in runs/*; do ls $r/*.pdb | wc -l; done
solution: for r in runs/*; do ls $r/*.pdb | wc -l; done

blocks.tip: Try a loop with `echo` first to see what it would do, then swap in the real command (like mv or rm) once the list looks right.

quiz.q: In `for f in *.pdb; do cp $f backup/; done`, what is `$f` the second time through?
quiz.why: f takes each matching file name in turn.
